explain.say: A bubble is a ball of air wrapped in a very thin skin of soapy water. When light hits it, some reflects off the outside surface and some off the inside surface.

explain.say: Those two reflections travel back as waves and overlap. For some colours the wave crests line up and the colour gets brighter; for others crests meet troughs and the colour cancels out.

faq.q: How thin is a bubble wall?
faq.a: A bubble wall is usually around a thousandth of a millimetre thick, and just before it pops it can be thinner than a ten-thousandth of a millimetre, hundreds of times thinner than a human hair.
asks: How thick is a soap bubble?

faq.a: Interference is what happens when two light waves overlap. If their crests line up they make brighter light; if a crest meets a trough they cancel. Thin films use this to pick out colours.
asks: What does interference mean in light?

faq.q: Why does a bubble go dark just before it pops?
faq.a: When the film gets extremely thin, the reflections from the front and back cancel out for all colours. So the thinnest part looks black or dark, a sign the bubble is about to burst.
asks: Why does a bubble get black spots?
What are the dark patches on a bubble?

faq.q: Why do the colours on a bubble move?
faq.a: Gravity pulls the soapy water down, so the film is thinner at the top and thicker at the bottom, and air currents stir it around. As the thickness changes, the colours shift and swirl.
asks: Why are bubbles different colours at the top and bottom?

faq.q: Why does oil on a puddle look rainbow-coloured?
faq.a: A thin layer of oil floating on water reflects light from its top and bottom surfaces, just like a bubble. Different thicknesses boost different colours, giving rainbow swirls.
asks: Why is a petrol puddle rainbow?

facts: Bubble colours come from thin-film interference between light reflected from the film's outer and inner surfaces.
Dark patches appear on a soap film when it becomes much thinner than the wavelength of light, shortly before it pops.
